claims.text: The investigated alloy is additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 with an fcc matrix.
Elevated-temperature degradation of this alloy is governed by the formation and stability of protective oxide scales.
The governing oxide-scale behavior is sensitive to oxygen partial pressure.
Oxidizing environments produce a coherent, adherent Al- and Cr-rich oxide scale on the target alloy.
An adherent Al- and Cr-rich oxide scale protects the fcc substrate from degradation.
Reducing atmospheres limit or disrupt protective oxide formation.
Failure to form or retain the protective scale under reducing conditions causes enhanced spallation and accelerated substrate degradation or oxidation.
Oxide-scale composition, thickness, and adhesion mediate degradation of the alloy.
Higher oxygen partial pressure will produce a more uniform and better-adhered oxide layer with a slower degradation rate than standard air.
Reducing atmospheres will produce thinner, discontinuous scales with more spallation and higher degradation rates than standard air.
In standard air at 800 °C, the target alloy initially reaches a balance between oxide-scale formation and limited spallation.
Scale spallation can occur during oxidation at 800 °C.
The selected exposures can be kept short enough that no phase transformation occurs beyond the stable fcc matrix.
Synergistic elemental effects can influence high-temperature oxidation behavior and oxidation kinetics.
Holding alloy composition and processing fixed while varying gas atmosphere provides a controlled comparison of oxygen-partial-pressure effects.
A lack of systematic differences in scale morphology, thickness, adhesion, and degradation rate among oxygen partial pressures would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
